title: QCDIAG: introducing cmd 0x10 logcodes
description:
Introduction of Get Log (DIAG_LOG_F 0x10) cmd code with limited basic code.

Additionally, it reuses some enums and value_strings from GSMTAP and GSM RR.

Please note, the development is ongoing and let me know if certain logical updates you would do on qcdiag related files (otherwise it makes it more complicated to me to streamline the changes). Some of the code might not make sense at the moment because it is added for future use and I do MRs for smaller code changes to make sure it's all ok.

[qcdiag.pcapng](/uploads/3247b14b2ae7f3db027798eec0dabd34/qcdiag.pcapng), [qcdiag_log.pcapng](/uploads/a52ede03e0531fbc959d229860fcc29b/qcdiag_log.pcapng)

Additional participants: @laf0rge, @osmith42, @lynxis

changed this line in [version 14 of the diff](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/23587/diffs?diff_id=1665293651&start_sha=e0dbffa4cfd9fec27ce0102c05f22997eb885d67#3f9bf15cbd698a6492dccf1870b37f8bad11b013_5_5)

There are no examples of either of the fields that use this in your capture, but I am so used to seeing Uplink=0  Downlink=1 I thought I'd check that this is the right way around?  I always found this type slightly confusing in that it is the true then the false values..

This case is correct.

There are GSM RR and GSM MAC packets where 0x00 is uplink and 0x80 is downlink. Yes, it is somehow opposite of the usual order and I am not sure what is the reason behind.

So this is not a mistake. 

For example, GSM MAC:

```c
enum gprs_mac_chan_type {
    PRACH_11BIT_CHANNEL = 0x01,  // Uplink
    PRACH_8BIT_CHANNEL  = 0x02,  // Uplink
    PACCH_RRBP_CHANNEL  = 0x03,  // Uplink
    UL_PACCH_CHANNEL    = 0x04,  // Uplink
    PPCH_CHANNEL        = 0x80,  // Downlink
    PAGCH_CHANNEL       = 0x81,  // Downlink
    PBCCH_CHANNEL       = 0x82,  // Downlink
    DL_PACCH_CHANNEL    = 0x83,  // Downlink
};
```

Packet 5:
```
Qualcomm Diagnostic, GPRS MAC Signaling Message (Downlink)
    Log Code: GPRS MAC Signaling Message (0x5226)
    Length: 37 bytes
    Command Code: Get Log (0x10)
    More log data available indicator: 0
    Log Message Length: 37 bytes
    Timestamp: Jan  6, 1980 07:00:00.000000000 SE Asia Standard Time
    GPRS MAC Signaling Message (Downlink)
        Channel Type: DL-PACCH (0x83).  <---
        1... .... = Direction: Downlink <---
        Message Type: 0x01
        Message Length: 22 bytes
```

I must have been bored when I added the --common-usage option, which shows that the uplink_downlink one isn't used that much:

./tools/check_tfs.py --common-usage | grep uplink
 
tfs_uplink_downlink used in 3 dissectors
(just noticing that { "Set", "Not set" } should have matched tfs_set_notset, will need to look into that)
The issue here with set_notset was that the references are all from plugins, that can't share data from libwireshark (at least under Windows?)

This looks alright to me if you can fix the spelling and check the true_false_string order?

I've done some fuzzing under valgrind, but there really isn't anything that looks dangerous.

Those 3 examples are actually just context information, rather than one bit out of a real/efficient protocol message, they are usually just found as a **whole** byte.

There is an option in check_tfs.py:

`  --check-value-strings
                        check whether value_strings could have been tfs?
`

I don't think it was ever all that useful, but looking at it again now, it will only flag value_strings whose strings/values match (will also note if they match but with different case), but also have mask of only 1 bit.  The cases you flagged above are all 8 bits with no mask - a TFS() field cannot default to ***"Unknown"***.

**Somehow**, I haven't been using markdown in gitlab comments, can see how *useful* `it really is`, trying it out a little bit in this message.
It's more clear, thanks for the explanation.
resolved all threads
